title: About
text:
I find beauty in mathematics, not only by its utility, but also on its results of theorems, lemmas, proofs, even its conjectures. An analogy I always make is that theorems and lemma are like magic tricks. The proof is teaching you how to do that magic trick! Yet, unlike most magic tricks, knowing how they work does not necessarily make them any less fascinating. Sometimes, it makes them even more beautiful.
Through this blog, I want to explore mathematical theorems and results that I personally find fascinating, and hopefully share some of that fascination with others. I will also tell you why do I think it is beautiful. It might not be a very fancy results, but somehow I find it beautiful. ## How I approach this blog Oftentimes, the resources I found in learning mathematic’s theorems, they are too complicated and unintuitive such that it requires a lot of preliminaries that leads to rabbit holes of resources to dig, which then frequently leads to those initial excitements of learning a new concept vanish.
Or it is made too shallow (usually, to reach a more general audience) but resulted in losing a lot of details and nuances that makes mathematics exciting!
This blog is my attempt to find a middle ground between these two approaches. I will explain results where its shallow enough to make sure readers can follow, while at the same time, deep enough to satiate mathematician’s curiosity hunger! Noting everyone’s hunger level are different, I will put my resources and further readings in each post.
Finally, to answer your question of “where would we use this theorem?”, I will occasionally put some examples of practical usages where the concept explained is used.



I am in no way an expert on mathematics. Equipped with a master’s degree that involves mathematics, along with immense passion for the subject, I will try my best to make each post as accurate, as helpful as possible. If you notice any mathematical errors, typos, or unclear explanations, please raise a GitHub Issue. Questions, corrections, and suggestions are always welcome!

title: Irrationality of Square Root of 2
text:
​ This is the first theorem that hooks me into mathematics. If you are studying real analysis using Stephen Abbot’s Understanding analysis (Abbott 2015), this is the first and foremost thing the author discusses. You might or might not be as impressed as I was when I first looked at this beauty of a proof, but mathematicians all admit that this is a beautiful proof due to its simplicity.
​ Although there are a handful of ways to proof it, I will provide one here that I find attractive.

Theorem 1 (Irrationality of \(\sqrt{2}\)) There is no rational number whose square is 2 (Abbott 2015).


Proof. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that \(\sqrt{2}\) is rational. Then there exist integers \(p\) and \(q\), with \(q \neq 0\), such that
\[
\sqrt{2} = \frac{p}{q},
\]
where \(p\) and \(q\) have no common factors other than 1. That is, the fraction \(\frac{p}{q}\) is in its lowest terms.
Squaring both sides, we obtain
\[
2 = \frac{p^2}{q^2},
\]
which implies
\[
p^2 = 2q^2.
\]
Thus, \(p^2\) is even. Since the square of an odd integer is odd, \(p\) must also be even.
Consequently, we can write \(p = 2k\) for some integer \(k\). Substituting this into the equation above gives
\[
(2k)^2 = 2q^2,
\]
and hence
\[
q^2 = 2k^2.
\]
Therefore, \(q^2\) is even, which implies that \(q\) is also even.
We have shown that both \(p\) and \(q\) are even. Hence, they are both divisible by 2, contradicting our assumption that \(p\) and \(q\) have no common factors other than 1.
Therefore, our original assumption must be false, and we conclude that
\[
\boxed{\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}.}
\]







TipChallenge: Can We Generalize This Result?



We have shown above that \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational. But is this property unique to the number 2? We know \(\sqrt{4} = 2\) so its rational. What about 3 or 5?
Challenge: Can we generalize this result to \(\sqrt{n}\) for any positive integer \(n\)? In other words, is the square root of every positive integer irrational?
If not, under what conditions is \(\sqrt{n}\) rational?
Hint: Consider the role of evenness in our proof. Can we replace it with a more general property of integers?
